rv.q: Jones is superb: ridiculous, loudly self-pitying, sarcastic — and desolate.
Ian Rickson's exquisite production is full of energy despite the play's prevailing ennui.

Like so many good versions of classics, Conor McPherson's new adaptation feels almost impossibly contemporary in the way it packs so much lust, wit, rage and regret into its brisk but unhurried two and a half hours.

I'm not sure I've seen any better catch the tragicomic mixture of fury and futility when – re-roused to ire at talk of the estate being sold-off – Jones's frantically unhappy nobody runs amok with a gun, then subsides into stunned apathy.
The alchemy of this retooled Vanya, combining a top-notch creative team with serious actors who are currently having A Moment, works brilliantly.
Jones is note-perfect: sad but also genuinely hilarious. He even manages to claw back some dignity confronting Hinds about his monstrous dickishness.
Ian Rickson's production is polished to a high shine... everything about it gleams, almost too much; it's too controlled, too tidy.
But the best thing about Ian Rickson's production of Anton Chekhov's maudlin masterpiece is a ravishingly bored, passionate and tender performance from Rosalind Eleazar as Yelena.
But the production is decked out with a fine cast... But Toby Jones's wonderfully funny Vanya is the real pay-off.

This new production is full of undeniable beauties, as you would expect from adapter Conor McPherson and director Ian Rickson — still, it misses Chekhov's apparently haphazard significance: it is too deliberate.
Every single player here evokes their character's ennui terrifically – but it is so dimly lit, the staging so staid, the pace so unhurried, that the ennui is catching.

Young Aimee Lou Wood, not long out of Rada, pretty much steals the show in Ian Rickson’s watchable but flawed Uncle Vanya. Wood plays Sonya, the self-doubting daughter in Chekhov’s household of failures. She is up against quite a cast: Toby Jones, Anna Calder-Marshall, Dearbhla Molloy, Peter Wight, Ciaran Hinds.
It is radical and revelatory without ever being gimmicky or insensitive.
It's a superlative collective performance from the cast – many of us will be lucky if we see a better one in our lifetimes.
This more conventionally staged version has a masterly sense of pace and place, with director Ian Rickson orchestrating a mostly stellar cast in a beautifully nuanced account of the play.

Overall, this new version of Uncle Vanya is entertaining, playing up and introducing comic moments wherever possible but keeping much of the spirit of Chekhov, while the new elements give it a more contemporary edge.
The press-night crowd seemed to love this version but to me it was a half-full Vanya.
Judged by Rickson own past record, this only intermittently touching and funny production is a disappointment.
But the new ideas attached to this classic feel like woolly thinking and the evening falls between the two stools of convention and invention.
